messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: "testify" functionality plans
parts:
Hi!

I have used the "testify" functionality from the rstan dev version and must say, it is really amazing! As it is not yet released, maybe some points to consider:

- ideally one could serialize these objects just as stan models; maybe one could change the way this is built to the way Stan models are handled?

- as I understood this trick relies on sourceCpp from Rcpp. In order to serialize this type of objects, the Rcpp developers recommend to build a package - would this be possible to implement? I.e. the idea would be to turn a Stan model into tiny R packages which come along with the model itself and the exported user functions. This would be really cool, if one could just say "build a R package from my Stan model(s)".

- in any case, a possibility to obtain the cpp file which get's sourced would be very useful in order to let users to build packages from it.

Anything in this direction would be great and would also be of great use to build packages which are around some Stan-based MCMC models.

Best,
Sebastian

PS: Combining this testify stuff with Vectorize from R makes posterior simulations in R really straightforward!

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: "testify" functionality plans
parts:
At the moment, this doesn't seem particularly feasible. The function formerly known as testify() throws away everything but the user-defined functions and makes a lot of changes to those anyway. But if you do

cat(stanc("model.stan", obfuscate_name = FALSE), file = "model.cpp", sep = "\n")

then you have a C++ file in your working directory that could be part of a package. You would just have to do a bit of work to export the relevant C++ functions and write R functions that called the C++ functions. To some extent this would be scriptable but there are no scripts yet.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] simulations and posterior predictive checks in Stan
parts:
Sebastian told me that there’s a function, I think Ben wrote, that allows you to run Stan functions from R. Using functions should be more convenient than having to write an entire Stan program with an empty model block. It is not urgent, I just think it will be very helpful.

Using the generated quantities block is perfect for simulation _after_ inference, but it’s not the most natural thing for simulating fake data from the prior, or for simulating new quantities given simulations from a previously-fitted model. For the latter, Daniel suggested a hack in R, but it should be possible to do it more directly.

A

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] simulations and posterior predictive checks in Stan

On Thursday, April 9, 2015 at 10:07:56 PM UTC+2, Andrew Gelman wrote:
I agree with Sebastian.  I’m simulating a lot of fake data and I’d love to be able to routinely to do this in Stan rather than having to write custom R code.  One very pleasant thing about simulation in Stan is that it treats everything as a random variable, hence no need to loop over #sims, no more rnorm(nsims,…), etc.  This could be a very big deal!

Hi,

This is for this sort of stuff that I wrote gsim. I think the current interface is a bit
awkward to use so I'm currently redesigning it in a dplyr fashion. Once it's complete
it will look like this:

sims <- mutate(stanfit,
  new_quantity = rnorm(mu_y, sd_y)
  new_quantity2 = my_var * new_quantity + other_param
)

with all looping taken care of behind the scene. Would this interface provide what you need?

Lionel

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] simulations and posterior predictive checks in Stan
parts:
I think the issue is that Andrew wants everything written in Stan,
ideally just once. What we want to avoid is any code duplication
at all. Barring that, we'd like to write everything in Stan itself.

Many of our users don't even use R, so an R-centric solution isn't
general enough for us, though could be helpful in the short run.

One thing Andrew's complained about is that R uses a different notation
(rnorm vs. normal), and has different parameterizations and syntax for
other operations like matrix ops. (I also think you're missing
a number of draws argument to your rnorm() call if that's meant to be in R).

- Bob

parts:
On Saturday, April 11, 2015 at 5:24:57 AM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
I think the issue is that Andrew wants everything written in Stan,
ideally just once.  What we want to avoid is any code duplication
at all.  Barring that, we'd like to write everything in Stan itself.

This makes a lot of sense, especially when it comes to publishing the final
form of a research. gsim is only really useful for exploration, which can't
really be done with Stan when the model takes a lot of time to converge.

One thing Andrew's complained about is that R uses a different notation
(rnorm vs. normal), and has different parameterizations and syntax for
other operations like matrix ops.   (I also think you're missing
a number of draws argument to your rnorm() call if that's meant to be in R).

Indeed, I wrote that too fast ;-).

One thing I'll add is a _rng family of functions such as normal_rng(). They will
be parametrised following BDA conventions. And they will have parameters as
their first arguments, so the number of draws can be omitted when it is 1. I'm
hoping there is some way to reuse the Stan c++ _rng functions but I haven't
investigated it much yet.

As for density functions, we can't really have normal(), binomial() etc in R
because a lot of those names are already taken. Thankfully they are not so
useful for model exploration anyway.


Lionel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] simulations and posterior predictive checks in Stan
parts:
gsim is not a stopgap, it's a way to do interactive data analysis
directly in R. Writing a Stan model to perform simple actions on
posterior draws looks a bit burdensome to me.

The current gsim interface is not great in that respect either
because you need to wrap a stanfit before doing computations, but
I expect the next version to be much more streamlined thanks to
a dplyr-like design.

messages.author: 074998f49d84156c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] simulations and posterior predictive checks in Stan
parts:
That said, I agree it would be great if Stan had natively the
ability to use previously sampled draws. Rather than a hack where
the draws are used as data inputs, it may make sense for Stan to
take explicitely such a sample as input to use one draw at each
step.

This could be used to perform simulations with r.v. parameters,
but I wonder if it could also be used in model fitting to account
for the uncertainty of previously estimated parameters, such as
multiple imputations. Would HMC behave well with this scheme?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] simulations and posterior predictive checks in Stan
parts:
> On Apr 15, 2015, at 4:11 AM, Lionel Henry <lione...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> That said, I agree it would be great if Stan had natively the
> ability to use previously sampled draws. Rather than a hack where
> the draws are used as data inputs, it may make sense for Stan to
> take explicitely such a sample as input to use one draw at each
> step.

We spent most of the Stan meeting yesterday talking about just
this feature, which Andrew really wants. Here's the summary of
what we want to do:

* write a generated quantities block, and
* evaluate it AFTER the samples are drawn from Stan

so that the results are the same as if it had been originally
included in the Stan program.

That way, you can play with different generated quanitities
computations without having to fiddle indexes the way you
have to do with extracted draws in RStan at the moment.

I think it's doable, but no idea when we'll get to it.
The major stumbling block now is the ability to read the
output CSV file back into structured inputs. If we could do
that, all we'd need to do is write the C++ code and figure
out how to plumb it through all the interfaces.

> This could be used to perform simulations with r.v. parameters,
> but I wonder if it could also be used in model fitting to account
> for the uncertainty of previously estimated parameters, such as
> multiple imputations. Would HMC behave well with this scheme?

We don't know --- it's an open research area related to
Michael's adiabatic sampling.

It's also somewhat related to the notion of cut() that our
friends in pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics want us to apply
in a BUGS-like fashion in the situation where they trust
their PK model but know their PD model is misspecified and
don't want the misspecified model distorting the well estimated
PK model that still has uncertainty.

- Bob
